A Sri Lankan soldier walks through Mullaittivu, the former military headquarters of the Tamil rebels. More than 200 civilians and at least 30 children have been injured in the last three days of fighting, a relief worker told CNN Sunday. "That is the absolute minimum (number of injured)," the aid worker, who did not want to be identified for fear of jeopardizing the work of relief organizations, said. Government officials are accusing aid organizations and foreign media of sensationalizing civilian casualties. "It looks as if it's convenient for certain agencies to exaggerate the numbers so that this can be converted to a humanitarian crisis in the public eye, " Secretary of Foreign Affairs Dr. Palitha Kohona told CNN. On Sunday, Sri Lankan Defense Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa promised to "continue with the military offensive until we liberate the remaining area under LTTE (the rebel group) control," according to Sri Lanka's state-run news agency.  Watch a report on civilians caught in fighting » . A "handful" of United Nations staff are working around the clock to save a growing number of children caught in the crossfire, a U.N. spokesman said Saturday. Children as young as 4 months old were being treated in local hospitals for shrapnel injuries and other "wounds of war," spokesman James Elder told CNN. "There is just intense fighting in a small area where children and other civilians are," Elder said. "The space (where conflict is taking place) is shrinking and the fighting is augmenting." Thursday, U.N. aid workers rescued 50 critically injured children and 105 adults, he said. "We are trying to get as many people out of there as we can," Elder said. Humanitarian groups say as many as 250,000 unprotected civilians are trapped in the area. Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has promised to allow safe passage to trapped civilians and urged the Tamil Tigers to promise the same. "We have declared a safe zone for civilians, the coordinates of which were announced by the security forces," Rajapaksa said on his government's Web site. "It is unfortunate that the (Tamil Tiger group) is exploiting this declared safe zone for civilians by placing their heavy artillery within the safe zone and using it as a launching pad to attack security forces and indiscriminately kill civilians." The fighting has created a "nightmarish" situation for civilians in the conflict zone, Elder said. An emerging shortage of humanitarian supplies and diminished access to clean water, sanitation, and food are compounding a crisis, he said. Sunday, Sri Lankan soldiers seized a key rebel stronghold in a surprise attack deep in Tamil held territory. Troops crossed a lagoon and entered the town of Mullaittivu before encountering heavy resistance from Tamil fighters, according to the government-run news agency. The The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) -- commonly known as the Tamil Tigers -- have fought for an independent homeland for the country's ethnic Tamil minority since 1983. The civil war has left more than 70,000 people dead.

He accused the Tamil Tigers of abusing that zone by positioning heavy artillery inside it and using it as a base from which to attack security forces and kill civilians indiscriminately.

Elder described conditions for civilians in the fighting area as “nightmarish.” He said the situation was being worsened by growing shortages of humanitarian supplies, along with reduced access to clean water, sanitation, and food.

**Artillery shells hit hospital in Sri Lanka war zone, killing civilians, U.N. says**

*Colombo, Sri Lanka* — Artillery shells struck a hospital in Sri Lanka’s northern Mullaittivu district amid heavy fighting between government forces and Tamil Tiger rebels, killing and wounding civilians trapped in one of the last rebel-held areas, United Nations officials and aid workers said.

The shelling hit the hospital as thousands of civilians remained caught between advancing Sri Lankan troops and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, in the island nation’s northeast. Medical staff said the facility had been treating war-wounded civilians, including women and children, when the shells landed nearby and on the hospital grounds.

The exact number of casualties could not be independently confirmed because access to the area has been severely restricted. U.N. officials expressed alarm over reports of civilian deaths and injuries and called on both sides to respect international humanitarian law, including the protection of hospitals, medical workers and civilians.

“The U.N. is deeply concerned about the safety of civilians trapped in the conflict zone,” a U.N. official said, urging both the Sri Lankan military and the Tamil Tigers to avoid firing into populated areas and to allow safe passage for noncombatants.

Sri Lankan officials denied intentionally targeting civilians or medical facilities. Military spokesmen said government forces were conducting operations against LTTE positions and accused the rebels of using civilians as human shields and firing from near hospitals and other protected sites.

“The security forces do not target hospitals,” a Sri Lankan government official said. “The responsibility for civilian suffering lies with the LTTE, which is preventing people from leaving.”

The Tamil Tigers, who have fought for decades for an independent Tamil homeland in northern and eastern Sri Lanka, blamed the government for the shelling and said civilians had nowhere safe to go as the army pushed deeper into rebel-held territory.

Humanitarian agencies have warned that food, medicine and clean water are running dangerously low in the conflict area. The U.N. and international aid groups have repeatedly called for a pause in the fighting to evacuate the wounded and allow emergency supplies to reach civilians.

The battle for Mullaittivu is part of the Sri Lankan government’s final offensive against the LTTE, which once controlled large portions of the north and east. The government says it is close to defeating the rebels militarily, but aid agencies warn the civilian toll is mounting as the front lines shrink and more people are crowded into a small area under fire.

counterfactuals.output:
**Mullaittivu, Sri Lanka — 2009: Civilians Trapped as Final Offensive Intensifies Amid Disputes Over Casualty Figures**

As Sri Lankan government forces pressed their final offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in early 2009, tens of thousands of civilians were trapped in a rapidly shrinking pocket of territory in the northeastern district of Mullaittivu, caught between advancing troops, entrenched rebel fighters, and a deepening humanitarian crisis.

The fighting marked the closing phase of Sri Lanka’s nearly three-decade civil war. Government troops, having recaptured much of the north, pushed into the LTTE’s last strongholds around Mullaittivu, including coastal areas where civilians had fled repeatedly as front lines shifted. The Sri Lankan government said it was conducting a “humanitarian operation” to free civilians held by the Tigers. Aid agencies and human rights groups, however, warned that civilians were facing indiscriminate danger from shelling, lack of food and medical supplies, and restrictions on movement.

## Civilians Caught in the Battle Zone

By the first months of 2009, large numbers of Tamil civilians were packed into makeshift camps, villages, and open areas near the northeastern coast. Many had been displaced multiple times and were living under tarpaulins or in bunkers dug into sand and earth.

The Sri Lankan government declared “No Fire Zones” intended to provide refuge for civilians, but international agencies and witnesses later reported that these areas also came under fire. The government denied deliberately targeting civilians and accused the LTTE of positioning fighters and heavy weapons near civilian concentrations.

The LTTE, for its part, was widely accused of preventing civilians from leaving the conflict zone, forcibly recruiting people, including children, and using civilians as a buffer against the military advance. The Tigers denied some accusations, but the United Nations and human rights organizations reported credible evidence that civilians who tried to escape were sometimes stopped or shot at by LTTE cadres.

For families trapped inside Mullaittivu, the distinction between military and civilian space reportedly collapsed. Hospitals, food distribution points, roads, and shelters were overwhelmed as the fighting closed in.

## Injured Children and Overwhelmed Medical Facilities

Medical workers operating inside the conflict zone described scenes of extreme distress. Children were among the most visible victims: wounded by shell fragments, gunfire, blasts, and collapsing shelters. Reports from local doctors and international agencies described children arriving at makeshift medical points with amputations, abdominal injuries, head wounds, burns, and severe blood loss.

Hospitals and temporary clinics lacked basic supplies. Doctors reported shortages of anesthetics, antibiotics, blood, bandages, surgical equipment, and fuel for generators. Operations were sometimes performed in overcrowded, poorly lit conditions, with patients lying on floors or outside under trees.

The government accused some local medical officials in LTTE-held areas of inflating casualty figures under rebel pressure. Several doctors who worked in the war zone later gave conflicting accounts after being detained and questioned by authorities, saying publicly that earlier casualty estimates had been exaggerated. After their release, some later indicated that their statements had been made under pressure, adding to controversy over the reliability of wartime information.

International monitors were largely absent from the battlefield, making independent verification extremely difficult.

## Humanitarian Access Severely Restricted

Humanitarian access became one of the most contentious issues of the offensive. In September 2008, months before the final battles, the Sri Lankan government ordered most international aid workers to leave LTTE-controlled areas, citing security concerns. As a result, international humanitarian agencies had little or no permanent presence inside the war zone during the worst stages of the crisis.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) remained one of the few organizations able to carry out limited evacuations by sea, transporting wounded civilians from the conflict area to government-controlled hospitals when conditions allowed. But access was intermittent and depended on security guarantees from both sides.

Aid convoys carrying food and medicine were sporadic and often delayed. Relief organizations warned that supplies entering the area were far below the needs of the trapped population. The government said it sent food and medicine into the conflict zone and accused the LTTE of seizing supplies, restricting civilian movement, and worsening the humanitarian emergency.

The United Nations repeatedly appealed for a pause in fighting to allow civilians to leave safely and for aid to reach those still trapped. The Sri Lankan government rejected calls that it viewed as interference or as giving the LTTE time to regroup, while maintaining that civilians could escape through designated routes.

## Disputed Death Toll and Accusations of Exaggeration

Casualty figures from the Mullaittivu offensive remain highly disputed. During the fighting, aid agencies, local health officials, and UN sources reported rising civilian casualties, sometimes based on fragmentary information from doctors or witnesses inside the battle zone. Because independent observers were not present, many estimates relied on indirect reporting.

The Sri Lankan government repeatedly accused aid groups, international officials, and pro-LTTE networks of exaggerating civilian casualty numbers to generate international pressure for a ceasefire. Officials argued that inflated figures were part of a propaganda campaign designed to rescue the LTTE from defeat.

Some government representatives also said civilian deaths were far lower than alleged and insisted the army had used restraint despite fighting an enemy embedded among civilians. The military maintained that it stopped using heavy weapons in civilian areas, though this claim was disputed by witnesses, UN material, and later investigations.

Aid organizations rejected claims that they were deliberately inflating figures, saying they were attempting to report a crisis under extremely restrictive conditions. Human rights groups argued that uncertainty over exact numbers did not negate evidence of large-scale civilian harm.

In later years, UN reviews and international investigations concluded that tens of thousands of civilians may have died in the final months of the war, though precise figures remain contested. The Sri Lankan government has disputed many of those findings.

## Competing Narratives of the Final Offensive

The Mullaittivu campaign became a defining episode in Sri Lanka’s postwar debate. To the government, the offensive ended terrorism and restored territorial unity after decades of suicide bombings, assassinations, child recruitment, and conventional warfare by the LTTE. To many Tamil survivors and international rights advocates, the final months represented a catastrophic failure to protect civilians and a period of alleged violations by both sides.

The LTTE’s conduct came under severe criticism, including allegations that it used civilians as human shields, shot escapees, conscripted children, and placed military assets near civilian areas. At the same time, Sri Lankan forces faced allegations of indiscriminate shelling, attacks affecting hospitals and civilian zones, denial of adequate humanitarian relief, and mistreatment of surrendering or captured individuals.

The absence of independent media and humanitarian observers inside the conflict zone during key stages contributed to continuing disputes over responsibility, scale, and intent.

## Aftermath

The war ended in May 2009 with the defeat of the LTTE and the death of its leader, Velupillai Prabhakaran. Hundreds of thousands of civilians who emerged from the battle zone were placed in heavily guarded displacement camps, most notably the Menik Farm complex, where access by journalists, aid groups, and relatives was initially restricted.

Many survivors carried physical and psychological injuries, including children who had lost limbs, parents, siblings, or homes. Questions over missing relatives, civilian deaths, alleged war crimes, and accountability remain politically sensitive in Sri Lanka and internationally.

The Mullaittivu offensive remains one of the most controversial chapters of the Sri Lankan civil war: a military victory that ended a brutal insurgency, but one shadowed by unresolved claims of civilian suffering, restricted humanitarian access, and bitter disputes over how many died in the final weeks.

counterfactuals.output:
# Humanitarian Crisis Deepens in Northern Sri Lanka as Civilians Trapped by War

*This article is a retrospective news-style account based on publicly reported events and statements from the final phase of Sri Lanka’s civil war in 2009. Quotes attributed to named public figures reflect widely reported remarks or public positions from that period; where exact wording cannot be independently verified here, statements are presented in paraphrase rather than as direct quotations.*

## Civilians caught between advancing army and retreating LTTE

Northern Sri Lanka was plunged into one of the gravest humanitarian crises in its modern history during the final months of the government’s military offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, as tens of thousands of civilians were trapped in a shrinking strip of territory along the island’s northeastern coast.

By early 2009, Sri Lankan government forces had captured much of the LTTE’s former de facto administrative heartland in the Vanni region, including Kilinochchi, the town long regarded as the Tigers’ political capital. As the army advanced eastward, the LTTE withdrew toward Mullaitivu district, taking with it large numbers of civilians or preventing them from leaving, according to the United Nations, aid agencies, and the Sri Lankan government.

The result was a catastrophic concentration of civilians in an increasingly small war zone, where food, medicine, shelter, sanitation, and clean water were scarce. Hospitals struggled to function under shelling and shortages. Makeshift clinics were overwhelmed by shrapnel wounds, burns, amputations, dehydration, and malnutrition. Families dug bunkers in sandy soil, lived under tarpaulins, and waited for lulls in fighting to search for water or bury the dead.

Aid agencies warned that civilians were being squeezed between two forces: a government army determined to end the war militarily and an LTTE fighting force accused of using civilians as a buffer and preventing them from fleeing.

## “A catastrophic situation”

UNICEF spokesman James Elder was among the international officials who repeatedly drew attention to the plight of children and families trapped in the combat zone. Speaking during the crisis, Elder described conditions facing civilians as catastrophic and warned that children were being killed, maimed, separated from their families, and deprived of basic care.

Aid workers said the humanitarian situation had deteriorated rapidly after international agencies were ordered out of the conflict area in late 2008, leaving only limited local staff, medical personnel, clergy, and civilians to report from inside. Convoys carrying food and medical supplies were intermittent and insufficient for the growing population crammed into the shrinking area.

One aid worker familiar with the emergency response described the conditions as “a nightmare of overcrowding, fear and exhaustion,” saying that civilians were surviving on meager rations while the wounded often had little more than basic bandages and painkillers. “People were arriving with horrific injuries, and there simply was not enough medicine, not enough staff, not enough space,” the worker said.

Another humanitarian official said the crisis was made worse by the lack of safe passage. “The single most urgent need was to get civilians out of the fighting,” the official said. “But people were terrified, trapped, and in many cases physically unable to move.”

## Government defends offensive as war on terrorism

The Sri Lankan government, led by President Mahinda Rajapaksa, defended the offensive as a necessary campaign to defeat one of the world’s most formidable insurgent and terrorist organizations. The LTTE had waged a decades-long war for a separate Tamil state in the north and east of the island, carrying out suicide bombings, assassinations, forced recruitment, and attacks on civilians, officials said.

Rajapaksa repeatedly insisted that the military campaign was directed at the LTTE, not at the Tamil population. In public remarks during the final stages of the war, he portrayed the offensive as a humanitarian operation intended to “liberate” civilians held by the Tigers. His government accused the LTTE of using civilians as human shields, firing from near civilian areas, and shooting people who tried to escape.

Sri Lankan officials also rejected international calls for a ceasefire, arguing that any pause would allow the LTTE leadership to regroup, rearm, or escape. Senior defense officials said the army had opened safe routes for civilians and had instructed troops to minimize civilian casualties, while blaming the LTTE for preventing civilians from leaving.

Government representatives framed the operation as the final stage of a war that had devastated the country for nearly three decades. They argued that ending the LTTE’s military control would bring lasting peace, restore government authority, and allow displaced people eventually to return home.

“The objective is to free our people from terrorism,” officials said in substance at the time, emphasizing that the state had a responsibility to defeat an armed group that had rejected previous peace processes and continued to hold civilians in the conflict zone.

## Allegations of shelling and civilian deaths

Despite government assurances, the final offensive drew intense international concern over reports of heavy shelling in civilian areas, including locations designated as “no-fire zones.” The government denied deliberately targeting civilians and disputed casualty estimates, saying the LTTE had manipulated figures and staged attacks for propaganda.

Medical workers and local sources inside the conflict zone, however, reported repeated incidents in which shells landed near hospitals, food distribution points, and densely populated civilian shelters. The UN and human rights organizations later documented credible allegations that both the Sri Lankan military and the LTTE committed serious violations of international humanitarian law.

For civilians, the distinction between front line and safe zone became increasingly meaningless. Many had already been displaced multiple times, moving from village to village as the army advanced. By the final weeks, thousands were packed into narrow coastal areas with little protection from artillery, mortars, small-arms fire, and aerial bombardment.

Doctors working in makeshift facilities reported operating without anesthetics, sterilized equipment, blood supplies, or adequate antibiotics. Children with blast injuries lay beside elderly patients suffering from dehydration and infected wounds. Bodies sometimes remained uncollected because shelling made movement dangerous.

Humanitarian workers said the crisis was compounded by deep uncertainty over the number of people trapped. Estimates varied widely, with the government often giving lower figures than the UN and aid groups. That uncertainty made it difficult to plan relief deliveries and heightened fears that the scale of suffering was being underestimated.

## LTTE accused of trapping civilians

The LTTE, which had once controlled large areas of northern Sri Lanka and maintained its own police, courts, taxation systems, and military units, was by this stage surrounded and weakening. As its territory collapsed, it forced civilians to retreat with its fighters, according to survivors, the government, and international organizations.

UN officials and rights groups accused the LTTE of forcibly recruiting civilians, including children, and of shooting at people who attempted to cross into government-controlled territory. The Tigers denied some allegations but had a long documented history of forced recruitment and coercion.

Aid workers said the LTTE’s conduct deepened the humanitarian disaster. “Civilians were not simply caught in the wrong place,” one relief official said. “Many were actively prevented from leaving. That made an already deadly battlefield far worse.”

At the same time, humanitarian organizations stressed that LTTE abuses did not relieve the government of its obligation to protect civilians. International law requires all parties to distinguish between combatants and noncombatants and to avoid disproportionate attacks, even when an enemy operates among civilians.

## International pressure grows

As reports of civilian casualties mounted, the United Nations, Western governments, India, and international aid agencies urged both sides to halt fighting long enough to allow civilians to escape and aid to enter. Calls for a humanitarian pause intensified as the noose tightened around the LTTE.

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and senior humanitarian officials expressed alarm over the number of civilians in danger. The UN called on the LTTE to allow civilians to leave and on the Sri Lankan government to avoid the use of heavy weapons in populated areas. UNICEF and other child-protection agencies highlighted the particular vulnerability of children, warning that thousands had been traumatized, wounded, or separated from family members.

James Elder and other UN spokespeople repeatedly emphasized that children were paying an unacceptable price. Aid agencies warned that malnutrition, untreated injuries, and disease could kill even those who survived the shelling.

Sri Lanka, however, resisted outside pressure, insisting that the campaign was nearing its end and that foreign governments did not fully appreciate the LTTE’s brutality. Officials argued that the Tigers had used ceasefires in the past to strengthen their military position and that a halt at the final stage would prolong the suffering.

## Flight, screening, and camps

As the LTTE’s lines began to break, tens of thousands of civilians fled toward government-controlled areas, often crossing lagoons, sand berms, minefields, or exposed terrain under fire. Many arrived exhausted, injured, malnourished, and traumatized. Families were split apart in the chaos.

The government placed many displaced civilians in heavily guarded camps, the largest of which was the Menik Farm complex near Vavuniya. Officials said screening was necessary to identify LTTE fighters hiding among civilians and to prevent suicide attacks or insurgent regrouping. They also said the camps were required to provide food, shelter, medical treatment, and registration after months of displacement.

Humanitarian organizations acknowledged the need to assist large numbers of displaced people but criticized restrictions on freedom of movement, limited access for aid agencies, and the slow pace of releases. Conditions in the camps were initially overcrowded, with shortages of sanitation, privacy, and medical care.

Government officials defended the system as temporary and necessary under the circumstances. They argued that demining, reconstruction, and security checks had to take place before civilians could return to their villages.

## A war’s end, but not an end to suffering

In May 2009, the Sri Lankan government declared victory over the LTTE after the deaths of its top leadership, including Velupillai Prabhakaran. For many Sinhalese in the south, the end of the war brought relief and celebration after decades of bombings, assassinations, and insecurity. For many Tamils in the north and diaspora communities abroad, it brought grief, uncertainty, and anger over the scale of civilian suffering.

President Rajapaksa presented the victory as the reunification of the country and the defeat of terrorism. He promised reconstruction and a future in which all communities could live under one flag. Government officials said the military campaign had saved civilians from LTTE rule and made peace possible.

But aid workers and human rights advocates said the humanitarian crisis left deep wounds that could not be healed by battlefield victory alone. They called for accountability, transparency, resettlement, psychosocial care, and political reconciliation addressing the grievances that had fueled the conflict.

“The fighting may end in a day,” one aid worker said, “but the trauma will last for years.”

## Legacy of the crisis

The final months of Sri Lanka’s civil war remain fiercely contested. The government maintains that it carried out a legitimate military operation against a ruthless armed group that held civilians hostage. Critics argue that the state used overwhelming force with insufficient regard for civilian life and later failed to provide full accountability for alleged abuses.

What is not in dispute is that civilians in northern Sri Lanka endured extreme suffering. They were displaced repeatedly, trapped in combat zones, deprived of essentials, and exposed to shelling and gunfire. Children were killed and wounded. Families disappeared in the chaos. Survivors emerged from the war carrying physical injuries, memories of terror, and unanswered questions about missing relatives.

The humanitarian crisis in northern Sri Lanka stands as a stark example of the cost of wars fought among civilian populations. It also underscores a central principle of humanitarian law: even when a state confronts an abusive armed group, civilian protection cannot be treated as secondary to military victory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an international news piece about shelling at a hospital in Mullaittivu, the government’s capture of a rebel stronghold, and the broader background of the LTTE conflict and Sri Lanka’s civil war.
counterfactuals.output:
**Shelling Hits Hospital in Sri Lanka’s War Zone as Government Claims Capture of Rebel Stronghold**

*Colombo, Sri Lanka* — Artillery shells struck a hospital in Sri Lanka’s northern Mullaittivu district, according to aid workers and local medical officials, as government forces pressed deeper into territory held by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, in one of the most intense phases of the country’s long civil war.

The reported shelling came as Sri Lanka’s military announced the capture of Mullaittivu town, long considered one of the Tamil Tigers’ most important strongholds and the heart of their remaining territory in the island’s northeast. The fall of the town marked a major symbolic and strategic victory for the government, which has vowed to defeat the separatist guerrilla movement militarily after decades of conflict.

Medical officials in the conflict zone said shells landed in or near hospital grounds, causing casualties among patients and civilians who had sought shelter there. Independent verification remained difficult because journalists and most international aid agencies have been barred from the front lines. The government has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians or medical facilities, while accusing the LTTE of using civilians as human shields and operating from populated areas.

Humanitarian organizations have expressed growing alarm over the fate of tens of thousands of civilians trapped in shrinking rebel-held territory. Aid workers say many families have been displaced multiple times by the fighting and are facing shortages of food, medicine and safe shelter. The International Committee of the Red Cross and United Nations officials have urged both sides to respect international humanitarian law and allow civilians to leave combat areas safely.

The Sri Lankan military’s advance into Mullaittivu follows months of battlefield gains in the north, including the capture of Kilinochchi, the LTTE’s former administrative capital. Government officials have portrayed the campaign as the final stage of a war to reunify the country and end terrorism. President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s administration has rejected calls for a ceasefire, arguing that previous pauses allowed the Tigers to regroup.

The LTTE, once one of the world’s most formidable insurgent organizations, fought for an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of Sri Lanka, saying the island’s Tamil minority faced systemic discrimination by the Sinhalese-majority state. The group built a conventional fighting force, naval wing and intelligence network, and was notorious for suicide bombings and political assassinations, including the killing of former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993.

Sri Lanka’s civil war began in 1983 after anti-Tamil pogroms known as “Black July,” though ethnic tensions had been rising for decades over language policy, education, employment and political representation. Successive governments and Tamil militant groups entered and abandoned negotiations over federalism, autonomy and power-sharing. A Norwegian-brokered ceasefire signed in 2002 briefly raised hopes for peace, but it collapsed amid renewed assassinations, abductions and military offensives. Full-scale war resumed in 2006.

The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced hundreds of thousands more. Both the Sri Lankan military and the LTTE have been accused by human rights groups of serious abuses, including indiscriminate attacks, forced recruitment, extrajudicial killings and restrictions on civilian movement.

With Mullaittivu now claimed by the government, the LTTE’s remaining fighters are believed to be confined to a narrow coastal area along with a large civilian population. Diplomats and aid agencies warn that the final battles could produce a humanitarian catastrophe unless civilians are protected and medical facilities are spared.

For the Sri Lankan government, the capture of a rebel bastion may signal the approaching end of the Tigers’ territorial control. But for civilians caught between artillery fire, military advances and LTTE restrictions, the immediate concern remains survival.
